newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Chaotic fighting rages north of Afghan capital.
newsitem.headline: Chaotic fighting rages north of Afghan capital.

text.p: A chaotic patchwork of fighting raged north of Kabul on Wednesday, with no sign that the expected bid by forces of the ousted government to retake the Afghan capital from their Taleban foes was imminent.

Warplanes, presumably Taleban, bombed the militarily-important town of Jabal os-Siraj for a second day on Wednesday, narrowly missing a command post from which former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood sometimes operates, witnesses said.

The sound of jets approaching triggered frantic anti-aircraft fire as truck-mounted guns attempted to bring the attackers down. One bomb landed harmlessly in a field near Masood's command post and another damaged a house in the area.
Jabal os-Siraj sits 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul astride the main highway linking the capital to northern Afghanistan.
Ten km (six miles) south of Jabal os-Siraj, planes also overflew the town of Charikar, drawing anti-aircraft fire and curses from local residents who had been bombed on the two previous days.
"We had nine persons killed and six wounded here on Monday from these bombs and they came again yesterday," said an elderly resident as jet engines screamed in the distance.
"This is the fault of Pakistan. They support the Taleban who are trying to enslave us."
The conservative Islamic Taleban forces have gained momentum swiftly in Afghanistan over the past two years and took Kabul on September 27 to the surprise of virtually everyone.
Since then Masood has regrouped, mended fences with some former foes, including Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum, and begun moving back into position to try to recapture the capital.
Masood's office issued an ultimatum to the Taleban on Wednesday, essentially warning them to withdraw from Kabul or face the consequences.

Dostum forces, who had been stationed well away from the fighting, were spotted in Jabal os-Siraj on Tuesday and were said by residents to have moved down into the Charikar area overnight. Reporters driving through the area on Wednesday were unable to find them.
While aircraft bombing runs triggered fear among the local population on Wednesday, the fighting that really mattered north of Kabul was occurring on the ground.
The picture was far from clear.
An aid worker who drove the main highway from Jabal os-Siraj into Kabul early on Wednesday radioed back that the route was virtually devoid of life, military or civilian.
A few hours later reporters who headed south along the same route were stopped by former government soldiers where the main highway forks to the northeast towards Bagram military airfield.

A driver coming north from Qara Bagh, about five km (three miles) to the south, said there was heavy fighting in that small market town, which sits astride the main highway. Reporters could hear the rattle of small arms fire.
The sound of heavy artillery rumbled in the distance from the direction of Bagram airfield, where forces loyal to Masood have been battling for the better part of a week.
"That's fighting at Bagram," Amir Asif, who commands former government troops in the volatile triangle between Qara Bagh, Bagram and Charikar, told Reuters.
"Some parts of Qara Bagh are controlled by us and some by the Taleban, but we hope it will be resolved today. We are still fighting at Bagram as you can hear but things are going well."

Asif said most of the fighting in recent days around Qara Bagh had been among local residents rather than troops from the Taleban or the former government. The towns seem to have shifted allegiances at least three times in the past week.

With fighting flaring up and dying down again along the highway north from Kabul, many civilians were on the move. Some headed north to safety, others headed back to their homes after one or more cold nights living rough.
Refugees clung to overloaded trucks piled high with bedding and people. A few others rode donkeys or horses with personal belongings strapped in brightly-coloured saddle-bags.
Moving more slowly on foot, but with equal determination, was a ceaseless, dusty shuffling of humanity: veiled women, men carrying children and young boys driving goats and sheep.
